title: Mother of the Buddhas
hookLine: the perfection of wisdom honored as the mother of all Buddhas

cards: A stone figure of a woman, seated, legs folded, back straight, eyes lowered. Her face is calm, the kind of calm that looks like listening.

In some images like this one she holds a book, or a lotus with a book resting on it. You might guess she's a queen, or a saint, or somebody's grandmother carved from memory. She isn't a person at all.
She's a teaching. The sutras from yesterday gave the perfection of wisdom a family name. They called her a mother.

teach.b: First, the name. In Sanskrit, the perfection of wisdom is prajnaparamita.

The Perfection of Wisdom in Eight Thousand Lines speaks of this wisdom as the mother of the Tathagatas, the mother of every Buddha. A Buddha isn't born a Buddha. A Buddha is someone who has come to see things as they are.
The seeing comes first, so the seeing is called the mother. Second, a picture the sutra gives. A woman with many children falls ill.
Her children, all of them, drop what they're doing to look after her, keep her warm, keep her safe, because she gave them life and showed them the world.

The Buddhas, the sutra says, care for the perfection of wisdom the same way: not because it needs them, but because it made them. Notice the direction. The great ones serve the teaching, not the other way round.
Later, artists gave the teaching a form: the goddess Prajnaparamita, seated in meditation. Some Buddhists bow to her image and chant her name.

Others take the mother as a figure of speech, a way of saying where awakening comes from. Both are found inside Mahayana, and the sutra's words fit either. Fourth, why a mother, and not a teacher or a ruler.
A mother doesn't make a child by giving orders. She carries, she waits, she lets something grow in its own time.

teach.h: IT GIVES BIRTH, IT DOESN'T COMMAND.
teach.b: Wisdom in these sutras works like that: not a rule you obey, but what quietly gives birth to a different way of seeing.
And the one who sees owes it something.

how: In Mahayana Buddhism the perfection of wisdom is honored as the mother of the Buddhas; in some communities people bow before images of the goddess Prajnaparamita and chant her name, and the wisdom sutras are recited.

games.q: what does “mother of the buddhas” mean?
o: the perfection of wisdom, called the mother of every Buddha
a goddess who protects mothers and their young children
Queen Maya, the woman who gave birth to the Buddha

games.q: the mother of Buddhas: tap the pairs.
p: what she holds in some images

s: the mother of the Buddhas is a woman in the Buddha's family
she's a teaching: the perfection of wisdom, given the shape of a mother.
in the sutra's picture, the Buddhas look after the mother
like children caring for a mother who is ill, because she gave them life and showed them the world.
every Buddhist sees Prajnaparamita as a goddess to bow to
some bow to her image; others take the mother as a figure of speech. both ways are found in Mahayana.

games.q: the sutra pictures a mother who falls ill. what do her many children do?
o: all of them care for her
games.why: they all look after her, because she gave them life and showed them the world. the sutra says the Buddhas care for the perfection of wisdom the same way.

practice: Bring to mind one good thing you have, a skill, a habit, a friendship, and follow it back: who taught it to you, what book, what room, what hard year? You don't have to find the very beginning; find one source and rest there.
If you bow, bow to it in your mind; if you don't, just let it be thanked.

wordCard.voice: Mother of the Buddhas. The perfection of wisdom, called in the sutras the mother of every Buddha, because seeing comes before the one who sees. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: the perfection of wisdom, called the mother of the Buddhas.

carryVoice: Your line: the mother of Buddhas. Even the Buddhas tend her, the way children tend a mother. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita, the chapter on showing the world (the perfection of wisdom as mother of the Tathagatas; the simile of the sick mother and her children)
